units.title: Unit 87 — Verb constructions 1
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 87. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Choose an -ing form after verbs such as enjoy, avoid, consider, recommend and suggest.
Use to + infinitive after hope, agree, intend, offer, attempt, promise and demand.
Build verb + preposition constructions, including think of, insist on, ask for and blame someone for.
Recognise the different patterns used with suggest, decide, pretend and accuse.
Avoid common errors in verb complementation and express plans, choices and preferences naturally.

items.pt: gostar de fazer algo; sentir prazer em fazer algo
items.example: I enjoy learning new words through short conversations.
items.note: Enjoy is followed by a noun or -ing form, not a to-infinitive.

items.pt: se importar em fazer algo; incomodar-se em fazer algo
items.example: Do you mind waiting here for a moment?
items.note: Mind + -ing is common in polite requests and questions.

items.pt: não se importar em fazer algo
items.example: I do not mind sharing my notes with you.
items.note: Not mind + -ing indicates that an activity is acceptable.

items.example: She likes walking through the park after work.
items.note: Like can take -ing; a to-infinitive is also possible in many contexts.

items.example: He dislikes travelling on crowded buses.
items.note: Dislike is commonly followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.pt: odiar fazer algo; detestar fazer algo
items.example: I hate being late for important meetings.
items.note: Hate can take an -ing form; a to-infinitive is possible in some uses.

items.example: We avoid driving through the centre at rush hour.
items.note: Use avoid + -ing, not avoid to do.

items.pt: imaginar fazer algo; imaginar-se fazendo algo
items.example: Can you imagine living in a different country?
items.note: Imagine is typically followed by an -ing form when visualising an activity.

items.pt: considerar fazer algo; pensar na possibilidade de fazer algo
items.example: They are considering moving closer to the station.
items.note: Consider + -ing expresses thinking carefully about an option.

items.example: I recommend booking a table before Friday.
items.note: Recommend + -ing is correct; recommend to book without an object is not.

items.example: Mia suggested taking the earlier train.
items.note: Suggest + -ing is correct; suggest to take is not the normal construction.

items.example: I prefer to speak to someone I already know.
items.note: Prefer can take a to-infinitive or an -ing form; the questionnaire uses the to-infinitive.

items.pt: estar a fim de fazer algo; ter vontade de fazer algo
items.example: Do you fancy going for a walk after lunch?
items.note: Informal British English; fancy + -ing. Introduced in the dictionary exercise.

items.example: My brother enjoys reading science magazines.
items.note: The -ing form is obligatory after enjoy: not enjoy to read.

items.pt: esperar fazer algo; ter esperança de fazer algo
items.example: I hope to visit my grandparents next month.
items.note: Hope + to-infinitive is used for desired future actions.

items.example: The team agreed to start the meeting early.
items.note: Use agree + to-infinitive for agreeing to an action.

items.pt: pretender fazer algo; ter intenção de fazer algo
items.example: She intends to apply for another position.
items.note: Intend + to-infinitive is used for a plan or purpose.

items.example: Oliver offered to carry the bags upstairs.
items.note: Offer + to-infinitive means volunteer to do an action.

items.example: They attempted to repair the bicycle without help.
items.note: Attempt is followed by a to-infinitive here and means try; it can sound formal.

items.example: I promised to send the documents before noon.
items.note: Promise + to-infinitive expresses a commitment to an action.

items.pt: exigir fazer algo; exigir o direito de fazer algo
items.example: The customer demanded to speak to the manager.
items.note: Demand + to-infinitive expresses a strong request to do something.

items.example: We planned to leave earlier, but the train was cancelled.
items.note: Plan + to-infinitive is a natural alternative to intend; reinforced in the answer key.

items.example: He decided to study medicine.
items.note: Decide + to-infinitive is introduced in the dictionary exercise.

items.example: We decided that we would stay an extra night.
items.note: Decide can also introduce a that-clause; that is sometimes omitted.

items.pt: fingir fazer algo; fingir estar fazendo algo
items.example: She pretended to understand the instructions.
items.note: Pretend + to-infinitive is one dictionary-exercise pattern.

items.example: He pretended that he had not heard the question.
items.note: Pretend can also take a that-clause; that can be omitted.

items.example: I asked the librarian for help with the catalogue.
items.note: Ask + person + for + noun; not ask someone help.

items.example: He asked for advice about his university application.
items.note: Ask for + noun. Advice is an uncountable noun.

items.pt: pensar em fazer algo; cogitar fazer algo
items.example: I am thinking of buying a used bicycle.
items.note: Think of + -ing means consider an option; think about + -ing is also possible.

items.pt: pensar em fazer algo; considerar fazer algo
items.example: She is thinking about taking a language course.
items.note: An alternative to think of + -ing; avoid think to go in this sense.

items.example: My friend insisted on paying for our tickets.
items.note: Use insist on + -ing, never insist in + -ing.

items.example: They blamed the driver for the delay.
items.note: Blame + person + for + noun/-ing; do not use blame someone of.

items.example: She blamed me for forgetting the reservation.
items.note: The preposition for is followed by an -ing form when the cause is an action.

items.example: The police accused the man of theft.
items.note: Accuse + object + of + noun or -ing form; introduced in the dictionary exercise.

items.example: She accused her neighbour of taking the parcel.
items.note: Accuse takes of before a verb in the -ing form.

items.pt: sugerir que algo seja feito; propor que
items.example: Sam suggested that we meet after lunch.
items.note: Suggest can also introduce a finite clause, with optional that; it does not take suggest someone to do something.

items.example: Might I suggest a quieter place for our conversation?
items.note: A more formal and polite suggestion construction shown in the dictionary box.

units.title: Unit 88 — Verb constructions 2
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 88. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Use advise, persuade, warn and remind with an object and the correct complement.
Distinguish verbs that introduce that-clauses from verbs that need an object first.
Use ask, tell, want, allow, expect, help and encourage with an object and infinitive.
Express statements, promises, realisations and suggestions with optional that.
Correct common errors with say/tell, suggest, recommend, allow and negative infinitives.

items.example: The doctor advised her to drink more water.
items.note: Advise + object + to-infinitive; not advise someone do something.

items.pt: persuadir alguém a fazer algo; convencer alguém a fazer algo
items.example: We persuaded Luca to join the class.
items.note: Persuade means make someone agree to act, often through discussion.

items.word: persuade someone not to do something
items.pt: convencer alguém a não fazer algo
items.example: I persuaded my brother not to sell his bike.
items.note: The negative not goes before the to-infinitive.

items.word: warn someone not to do something
items.pt: avisar alguém para não fazer algo; alertar alguém a não fazer algo
items.example: The guide warned us not to touch the broken glass.
items.note: Warn + object + not to-infinitive tells someone to avoid a possible danger.

items.example: Please remind me to collect the parcel tomorrow.
items.note: Remind + object + to-infinitive helps someone remember a future task.

items.pt: pedir a alguém para fazer algo
items.example: I asked Marco to close the window.
items.note: Ask + person + to-infinitive; not ask that Marco close in ordinary conversational English.

items.pt: dizer a alguém para fazer algo; mandar alguém fazer algo
items.example: The instructor told everyone to wait outside.
items.note: Tell + object + to-infinitive gives an instruction.

items.example: We want the children to feel comfortable.
items.note: Use want + object + to-infinitive, not want that someone does something.

items.example: The museum allows visitors to take photos.
items.note: Allow + object + to-infinitive; do not omit to.

items.example: I expect the engineers to finish the test today.
items.note: Expect + object + to-infinitive describes what you think will happen.

items.example: The assistant helped me to find a suitable course.
items.note: Help + object + to-infinitive is correct; the to may also be omitted.

items.example: My sister helped me prepare for the interview.
items.note: Help is unusual here because both with and without to are correct.

items.pt: incentivar alguém a fazer algo; encorajar alguém a fazer algo
items.example: Our teacher encouraged us to speak more English.
items.note: Encourage + object + to-infinitive gives support or confidence.

items.pt: avisar alguém de que; alertar alguém que
items.example: They warned us that the road might be closed.
items.note: Warn + person + (that) + clause provides information about a possible problem.

items.example: He reminded me that the deadline was Friday.
items.note: Remind + object + (that) + clause brings information back to someone’s attention.

items.pt: perceber que; dar-se conta de que
items.example: I realised that I had left my keys at home.
items.note: Realise + (that) + clause means become aware of a fact.

items.example: I promised her that I would call after work.
items.note: Promise can take an optional recipient before its that-clause.

items.example: They promised that the repairs would be finished soon.
items.note: Promise + (that) + clause can occur without a recipient.

items.example: She suggested that we meet in the library.
items.note: Suggest + (that) + clause, or suggest + -ing; avoid suggest us to go.

items.example: Elliot mentioned that he was starting a new job.
items.note: Mention + (that) + clause introduces a fact, often briefly.

items.example: Nina suggested going for a walk after dinner.
items.note: Alternative pattern shown in the language-help box; there is no suggest + person + to-infinitive.

items.example: It was an opportunity to work abroad for a few months.
items.note: A chance to do something; prominent in the story heading.

items.example: I noticed that the lights were still on.
items.note: Notice + (that) + clause reports something observed.

items.example: The manager said that the office would be closed.
items.note: Say + (that) + clause does not take an indirect-person object here; say to me or tell me, not say me.

items.pt: esperar que; ter esperança de que
items.example: I hope that the weather improves before the trip.
items.note: Hope can be followed by an optional that-clause or by a to-infinitive for your own hoped-for action.

items.example: I recommend that we leave before the traffic gets heavy.
items.note: Recommend + (that) + clause; recommend + -ing is another correct pattern.

items.example: I expect that the package will arrive tomorrow.
items.note: Expect + (that) + clause expresses an expectation; compare expect someone to do something.

items.pt: dizer a alguém que; contar a alguém que
items.example: I told my colleague that the meeting was cancelled.
items.note: Tell needs an object when giving information to a person: tell me, not tell it is impossible.

items.example: The chart showed us that sales had increased.
items.note: Show + object + (that) + clause presents evidence or makes something clear.

items.example: She convinced her friends that the route was safe.
items.note: Convince + object + (that) + clause means cause someone to believe something.

items.example: She said a few words to the new students.
items.note: Use say something to someone, but tell someone something.

items.pt: contar algo a alguém; dizer algo a alguém
items.example: Please tell me the reason for the delay.
items.note: A person is the direct object after tell in this construction.

items.example: I recommend taking a short break after lunch.
items.note: This alternative avoids the incorrect pattern recommend to do something.

items.example: The guide advised us to leave before dark.
items.note: Advise + object + to-infinitive differs from recommend + -ing or recommend + that-clause.

items.pt: não fazer algo; para não fazer algo
items.example: I warned the children not to climb the wall.
items.note: Put not before to in negative infinitive complements after warn and similar verbs.
